item.content:encoded:
Sept. 22 is a notable date in Los Angeles Dodgers franchise history for multiple reasons, and also for the 1957 Brooklyn team because of Duke Snider.
On the final day of the regular season that year, Snider slugged two home runs in a 7-3 win against the Philadelphia Phillies. That gave Snider a fifth consecutive season with at least 40 homers, which tied Ralph Kiner’s National League record.
That wound up being Snider’s last prolific power season as he never surpassed 23 homers for the remainder of his career, which ended with the San Francisco Giants in 1964.
Beginning with Brooklyn in 1947, Snider played 16 seasons with the Dodgers organization. He earned seven consecutive All-Star Game selections during that span and finished in the top-10 in NL MVP voting in five of those seasons.
Dodgers history: Sept. 22
Sutton reaches 20 wins
On Sept. 22, 1976, Don Sutton threw a complete game against the San Francisco Giants at Candlestick Park to earn his 20th win of the season. He tacked on another victory that year but it wound up being the Hall of Famer’s first and only season reaching 20 wins.
Sutton passed away in January 2021 and was among those honored during the Hall of Fame ceremony this year.
Valenzuela makes history as Mexican pitcher
Ten years after Sutton reached 20 wins, Fernando Valenzuela accomplished the same feat by holding the Houston Astros to just two hits in a Dodgers’ 9-2 victory at the Astrodome. Valenzuela became the first Mexican pitcher to win 20 games in a single season.
Dodgers franchise home run record
After setting a franchise record with 221 home runs during the 2017 season, the Dodgers broke that mark on Sept. 22, 2018, when Yasmani Grandal slugged the team’s 222nd long ball in the sixth inning of a 7-2 win over the San Diego Padres.
The Dodgers finished with 235 home runs that season, then shattered it to set a new franchise high and NL record with 279 in 2019.
Jarrín immortalized at Dodger Stadium
On Sept. 22, 2019, the Dodgers held a pregame ceremony to induct Spanish-language broadcaster Jaime Jarrín into the Dodger Stadium Ring of Honor.
Pepe Yñiguez, Fernando Valenzuela and Hall-of-Fame broadcaster Vin Scully were among those to speak during the festivities.
Jarrí became the 12th person inducted into the Ring of Honor, joining Scully, Pee Wee Reese, Tommy Lasorda, Snider, Jim Gilliam, Sutton, Walter Alston, Sandy Koufax, Roy Campanella, Jackie Robinson and Don Drysdale.

SANTO DOMINGO, RD (Nelson de la Rosa–Prensa CBPC).- El 22 de septiembre de 1986, Fernando Valenzuela volvió a colocar su nombre en la historia del béisbol mexicano al alcanzar una cifra que hasta entonces ningún lanzador nacido en ese país había conseguido en las Grandes Ligas.
Hace exactamente 40 años, el zurdo de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles derrotó 9-2 a los Astros de Houston en el Astrodome para convertirse en el primer pitcher mexicano con 20 victorias en una temporada de MLB.
Valenzuela recorrió las nueve entradas, permitió solamente dos imparables y dos carreras —una limpia—, concedió tres boletos y ponchó a cinco. Incluso colaboró a la ofensiva con un sencillo productor.
Terminó aquella temporada con récord de 21-11 y efectividad de 3.14, completando 20 de sus 34 aperturas. Tal resultado lo mantuvo en la lucha por el Premio Cy Young de la Lia Nacional, donde finalmente terminó en el segundo lugar.
Pero la historia de Fernando no se limitó a las Grandes Ligas. La Serie del Caribe también formó parte de su extraordinaria trayectoria.
Cuatro años antes de aquella victoria número 20, Valenzuela había regresado a México convertido ya en una de las grandes figuras del béisbol. Venía de una inolvidable temporada de 1981 con los Dodgers, en la que conquistó el Premio Cy Young, el Novato del Año y la Serie Mundial.
En febrero de 1982 reforzó a los Naranjeros de Hermosillo en la Serie del Caribe celebrada precisamente en esa ciudad. Y allí protagonizó una de sus actuaciones más recordadas en el clásico regional.
Frente a los Leones de Ponce de Puerto Rico retiró a los primeros 17 bateadores que enfrentó y mantuvo el juego sin imparables hasta el octavo episodio en una victoria mexicana 14-0. MLB recoge aquella actuación al repasar la trayectoria caribeña del zurdo.
Valenzuela disputó tres Series del Caribe: en 1982 y 2001 con los Naranjeros de Hermosillo y en 1993 como refuerzo de los Venados de Mazatlán. En sus tres participaciones terminó invicto, con marca de 1-0 y efectividad de 1.05.
Su última aparición resulta particularmente significativa. En Culiacán 2001, con 40 años, “El Toro” volvió a vestir el uniforme de Hermosillo en el torneo regional, casi dos décadas después de aquella primera participación de 1982.
La huella que dejó en el clásico caribeño recibió posteriormente uno de sus mayores reconocimientos: en 2013 Fernando Valenzuela fue exaltado al Salón de la Fama de la Serie del Caribe, junto a figuras como Ricardo Carty, Tony Peña y Candy Maldonado.
Cuarenta años después, aquel triunfo número 20 en la MLB permanece como otra de las grandes fechas de una carrera que dejó huella a ambos lados de la frontera y también en la historia del béisbol caribeño.
Fotos: Getty Images /Archivo CBPC

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers are the National League West champions.
Again.
They have won their division 13 times in the last 14 seasons, and the one time in that period in which they didn’t, they won a then-club-record 106 games.
Somewhere along the way, the Dodgers did the impossible: They met the requirements to become the sports franchise Los Angeles demanded.
Appreciating what this means requires an understanding of how Shaquille O’Neal and Kobe Bryant transformed this city in the early 2000s,
With O’Neal and Bryant as their stars, the Lakers didn’t just win championships.
They were unbeatable.
This image was reinforced by the play of O’Neal, a 7-foot-1, 325-pound freak of nature who literally couldn’t be stopped.
By the time the Lakers completed their three-peat in 2002, championships were no longer something Los Angeles hoped for.
They became something the city expected.
This is the standard used to measure teams with aspirations of becoming a cultural touchstone in this congested market. With plenty of other entertainment options, casual fans won’t invest too much of their time and money in a team unless they believe it will create the kind of citywide pride O’Neal’s Lakers once did.
The Lakers haven’t been that team for some time. The Rams are producing a worthy on-field product, but they remain in the process of winning back fans they lost over the two decades they spent in St. Louis.
The Dodgers are the one team in town that is clearing the bar.
“What’s funny is Los Angeles has always been looked at, as far as sports, (as) a Laker town,” manager Dave Roberts said. “I think we might have the market share right now in Los Angeles. It’s great. I think we draw more fans than anyone in the world, obviously, with the home dates we have. But it’s 40,000, 50,000 every night. We travel well. I do think the guys see it. They feed off it.”
The Dodgers managed to do this despite playing a sport that is particularly hard to dominate. The Lakers could dump the ball into O’Neal 30 times a game. The Dodgers have employed a number of Hall of Famers over the years, but as great as Shohei Ohtani is, he can only hit four times a game, maybe five.
The Dodgers have become a different kind of juggernaut.
With substantial investment from their owners, they have built some of the deepest rosters in baseball history. In its first season operating the team, Guggenheim Baseball Management signed All-Star outfielder Andre Ethier to an $85 million extension, picked up a then-unknown Yasiel Puig for $42 million, traded for All-Star infielder Hanley Ramirez and assumed more than $260 million in contract obligations in a blockbuster trade for Adrian Gonzalez, Carl Crawford and Josh Beckett.
Season after season, the Dodgers fielded one of the most expensive teams in the major leagues — if not the most expensive team.
Which is why at some point in each of the last 14 seasons, the Dodgers were considered favorites to win the World Series.
They are well into their second decade as baseball’s model franchise — or, depending on the perspective, Evil Empire. The last time they didn’t reach the playoffs, the world was a completely different place. LeBron James had just won his first NBA championship. “Gangnam Style” was a global phenomenon. The recreational use of marijuana was still outlawed in every jurisdiction of the United States.
There’s an entire generation of fans who don’t know what it’s like for the Dodgers to not be legitimate contenders.
Consistency by itself didn’t turn the Dodgers into the Dodgers of today. Actually winning championships was important, of course, and doing that required them to adjust how they built their rosters.
President of baseball operations Andrew Friedman used to operate as if the playoffs were a crapshoot. The organization’s focus was on the regular season, on just reaching the postseason. Because depth is required to survive a 162-game schedule, quantity was emphasized over quality.
The approach didn’t produce any championships. The Dodgers reached the World Series twice in their first eight seasons under Guggenheim ownership but lost both times.
The failures prompted them to pursue real difference-makers.
Mookie Betts, who was the catalyst of the championship team in 2020. Freddie Freeman, the home run hero of the 2024 World Series. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, the Most Valuable Player of the 2025 World Series. And, of course, Ohtani, the franchise’s most transformative player since Fernando Valenzuela, or maybe even Jackie Robinson.
The Dodgers have won three of the last six World Series.
Even with Ohtani dealing with right arm and left knee injuries, they will open the postseason as the odds-on favorites to win their third consecutive championship.
As fragmented as Los Angeles can be, most of the city can get behind that.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have a long line of notable pitchers and on this day in franchise history, those stars shined a little brighter throughout the years.
On Sept. 17, 1963, Sandy Koufax pitched a shutout against the St. Louis Cardinals at Sportsman’s Park while giving up just four hits.
The shutout was his 11th of the season, which set a new National League record for the most in one year by a left-hander in MLB history. Grover Cleveland Alexander held the Major League Record with 16 shutouts during the 1916 season for the Philadelphia Phillies.
Also on this day in Dodgers history but during the 1981 season, Fernando Valenzuela threw his eighth shutout of the year with a three-hitter against the Atlanta Braves.
With eight shutouts, Valenzuela tied the rookie record that was set by Chicago White Sox pitcher Ewell Russell in 1913. In addition, Valenzuela broke the previous NL mark shared by Irving Young (Boston Beaneaters, 1905), Grover Cleveland Alexander (Phillies, 1911), and Jerry Koosman (New York Mets, 1968).
Dodgers history: Sept. 17
Nomo no-hitter
In 1996, 15 years after Valenzuela and 33 years after Koufax set their shutout records, Hideo Nomo threw the only no-hitter in history at Coors Field. It was one of two Nomo tossed during his 12-year career.
Nomo’s historic game came with the club locked in a pennant race and it was the 20th no-hitter in franchise history.
Joe Torre retires
Also on this day in Dodgers history, manager Joe Torre announced he will retire following the end of the 2010 season. He finished his career with a record of 2326-1997 (.538) during his 30 seasons as a skipper with Mets, Braves, Cardinals, New York Yankees, and the Dodgers.
The Dodgers then announced the team’s hitting coach Don Mattingly was hired to replace Torre, who accepted a position to assist Major League Baseball Commissioner Bud Selig as the new Executive Vice President for Baseball Operations.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers may have spoiled Josue De Paula's breakout game, but his monster home run against the Miami Marlins on Sunday sent a message: this kid may live up to his billing as LA's No. 1 prospect.
The Dodgers still have to figure out how they're going to fit him on the roster when Shohei Ohtani comes off the IL, but as long as his brief audition at the tail end of this season continues to go well, that should be a priority this offseason.
Maybe we're getting way ahead of ourselves here, but if the Dodgers figure out how to get him regular at-bats in 2027, we could be looking at the next in a long and storied line of Dodgers Rookie of the Year Award-winners.
The Dodgers have an MLB-leading 18, beginning, of course, with Jackie Robinson in 1947, the man the award is named after. Their latest winner was Cody Bellinger in 2017.
Sandwiched in between are franchise legends Jim Gilliam, Fernando Valenzuela, Eric Karros, and Hideo Nomo, just to name a few. De Paula could find himself in some very good company by the end of 2027.
Putting Josue De Paula's future Rookie of the Year campaign into context with other Dodgers greats
De Paula has been compared heavily to Yordan Alvarez, probably Andrew Friedman's greatest trade regret as the Dodgers' chief executive. Of the 12 position player Rookies of the Year the Dodgers have produced, none are quite the same archetype as Alvarez — David Ortiz, Kyle Schwarber-esque players who can flat-out hit.
But perhaps the most apt comparison is Mike Piazza, LA's winner in 1993. Piazza came into the league with far fewer expectations attached than De Paula, but both are defensively weaker position players with massive power potential and advanced plate discipline. De Paula has yet to strike out in the four games he's appeared in.
It would be unfair to expect the same kind of offensive production from De Paula that Piazza offered up in his rookie season, when he hit .318 with a .932 OPS, 35 homers, and 112 RBI to kick off what would become a Hall of Fame career.
But when the Dodgers, who are usually so enthused about their prospects, were all but champing at the bit to find him a place to play this season, that says a lot as to where they think his ceiling could be.
